With a real .tess/gate/signoffs/credentials.signoff.json artifact added, the SAME change clears (blocked=False) — proving this is a real escape valve (human sign-off), not the hard floor being permanently unusable.

outcomes.name: shape attacks — master-key glob, empty verifier_keys, expired key
outcomes.description: Three related fail-closed-by-shape checks: an over-broad covers_paths glob, a registry with no key for the claimed verifier, and a key that is already expired.
outcomes.mechanism: master_key_glob: BLOCKED — should be rejected at schema/lint time (HIGH-1(b), 'is_overbroad_glob') before it ever reaches covering-verdict discovery | empty_verifier_keys: BLOCKED — a real signature with nowhere to be checked against must fail-closed, not fail-open | expired_key: SLIPPED — the key's Expire-Date (2020-01-01) is already in the past at signing AND verification time; `_gate_verify_verdict_signature` / `_parse_gpg_fingerprint` only parse gpg's VALIDSIG status line and check fingerprint equality — they do not inspect gpg's EXPKEYSIG/KEYEXPIRED classification at all. Empirically: the gate SHIPPED it — an expired verifier key's signature still verifies. This is a REAL, disclosed gap: key expiry/revocation is not enforced by the signature check; the only mitigation today is manually removing a compromised/expired verifier's entry from policy.verifier_keys.

reasons: [contract] [verdict] verdicts/master-key.verdict.md $.covers_paths: ['**'] act(s) as a blanket 'master key' glob that would match every path in the repo (or every root-level path, for a bare '*') regardless of what this verdict actually reviewed — a verdict must scope covers_paths to the specific paths it reviewed, never a blanket glob
